name: Procyanidin oral (melasma)

lead: Oral procyanidin, a plant polyphenol, is taken together with vitamins A, C and E to fade melasma, the brownish facial patches that make skin tone look uneven. The payoff people want is a more uniform complexion on the cheeks and face, worked on from the inside rather than with a cream.

The idea is that antioxidant activity reduces the pigment behind the patches. An 8-week placebo-controlled trial in 56 women with epidermal melasma reported improvement on the cheeks. That is the one trial in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is taken as a daily supplement over several weeks, the length of the reported trial, and is usually thought of as a complement to sun protection and topical melasma care. Users look for gradual fading of patches rather than a quick change.

The trial summary describes the regimen as safe and well tolerated. Long-term safety data were not found. Melasma patches commonly darken again with sun exposure, so people usually pair any approach with sunscreen.

chain: Antioxidant pill with vitamins A, C, E
angle.text: Users take oral procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E to fade melasma patches and even out facial skin tone from the inside. The antioxidant combination is meant to reduce pigment in the skin, and an 8-week placebo-controlled trial in 56 women reported improvement on the cheeks.

lead: Oral procyanidin combined with vitamins A, C and E is a supplement regimen that has been tested for melasma, a facial hyperpigmentation disorder. Wikipedia's melasma article lists it among oral options, citing an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 56 Filipino women with epidermal melasma [1].

That trial reportedly found significant improvement in the malar (cheek) regions, and the treatment was described as safe and well tolerated [1]. The sources reviewed contain only this one summary, with no independent replication.
infobox: Procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E [1]

paras: Oral agents for melasma named by Wikipedia include tranexamic acid, procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E, and, from a systematic review, Polypodium leucotomos extract, beta-carotenoids and melatonin, which the review found effective with few and mild adverse events [1]. Standard care generally centers on topicals, sun avoidance and broad-spectrum sunscreen [1].

An 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 56 Filipino women with epidermal melasma reported significant improvement in the malar regions with procyanidin plus vitamins A, C and E, and good tolerability [1]. Details such as dose, effect size and funding are not given in the source reviewed, and no other trials were found.
